subject: accountancy
chapter_title: Trial Balance and Rectification of Errors

concepts.title: Meaning and Preparation of Trial Balance
concepts.definition: A trial balance is a statement of the debit and credit balances of all ledger accounts taken out on a date, prepared to test the arithmetical accuracy of the books, where the two columns must agree in total.
concepts.key_idea: The equality of the two sides proves that double entry has been applied throughout, though it does not certify the absence of all errors.

concepts.title: Objectives and Limitations of the Trial Balance
concepts.section: 6.2 Objectives of Preparing the Trial Balance
concepts.definition: The trial balance ascertains the arithmetical accuracy of ledger accounts, helps in locating errors, and provides the basis for preparing final accounts; yet errors of principle, complete omission and compensating errors do not disturb its agreement.
concepts.key_idea: A tallied trial balance is only a presumption of accuracy, since several classes of errors leave the two sides equal.

concepts.title: Classification of Errors: Omission, Commission, Principle and Compensating
concepts.definition: Accounting errors are classified as errors of complete or partial omission, errors of commission such as wrong posting or casting, errors of principle that break the accounting rules, and compensating errors that cancel one another.
concepts.key_idea: Classifying an error first decides whether it can be rectified through the suspense account or needs a correcting journal entry.

concepts.title: Rectification through the Suspense Account
concepts.definition: One-sided errors that leave the trial balance suspended are rectified through the suspense account, while two-sided errors are rectified by a journal entry that cancels the wrong effect and records the right one.
concepts.key_idea: The suspense account carries the trial balance difference until all one-sided errors are located and rectified, after which it closes automatically.

concepts.title: Rectified Totals after Correction of Errors
concepts.definition: After a wrong amount is replaced, the corrected total follows by deducting the excess or adding the shortfall from the old total, as when a purchase book is overcast or undercast.
concepts.key_idea: Overcasting inflates a total by the excess, so the rectified figure is the wrong total less the excess; undercasting works in reverse.
